The States General of the United Provinces of the Netherlands grant the Dutch West India Company a North American colony (New Netherland) including all of present New Jersey.

The New Sweden Company competes with the Dutch for control of trade in the Delaware Valley.
Swedish settlers arrive in the Delaware Bay aboard the ships Kalmar Nyckel and Fogel Grip and begin the colony of New Sweden.
Swedes control trade and settlement in the Middle Delaware Valley.
The Dutch capture New Sweden and absorb the Delaware Valley within New Netherland.
The English capture New Netherland, and King Charles IIs brother  James, Duke of York grants New Jersey to Sir George Carteret and John, Lord Berkeley.
The Dutch regain control of the Lower Delaware Valley for one year before it is recaptured by the English.
Seeking refuge from religious persecution in England, Quakers John Fenwick and Edward Byllynge buy West New Jersey from John, Lord Berkeley.
Proprietors John Eldridge, Gawen Lawrie, Nicholas Lucas, William Penn and Edward Warner organize to govern the province of West New Jersey.
Quaker settlers purchasing land rights from the Proprietors, arrive at Burlington aboard the Kent.
Mahlon Stacy builds one of the first gristmills in the Delaware Valley on the Assunpink Creek.
William Penn begins construction of his house at Pennsbury Manor roughly five miles below the Falls of the Delaware.
A Quaker monthly meeting convenes for the first time at the Falls of the Delaware in the house of William Biles near present day Morrisville.
The Society of Friends establishes a Quaker burying plot in what is today Riverview Cemetery.
Nottingham Township becomes the first municipal entity to encompass portions of the land that comprises modern day Trenton.
Floods destroy many of the homes at the Falls of the Delaware.
Burlington County establishes its boundaries and includes the Falls of the Delaware within its jurisdiction.
The Proprietors of East and West Jersey relinquish the government of the provinces to Queen Anne, and New Jersey becomes a Royal Colony.
Hunterdon County forms from the northern portion of Burlington County with the Assunpink Creek serving as a boundary
William Trent, merchant of Philadelphia, builds the brick mansion, today known as the Trent House, on land purchased from Mahlon Stacy, Jr.
William Trent and Samuel Green establish a water-powered ironworks on the Assunpink Creek at Trents Town
James Trent, son of William Trent, receives a royal charter for the operation of a ferry across the Delaware River
King George II grants Trenton status as a Royal borough
Trenton citizens form the Union Fire Company, the towns first volunteer fire group
The Trenton Library Company, founded by Dr. Thomas Cadwalader, opens the first subscription library in New Jersey
The colonial government authorizes the construction of the Trenton barracks to house soldiers fighting in the French and Indian War
General Washington crosses the Delaware River and marches south, defeating Hessian troops deployed by the British at the First Battle of Trenton
American forces led by George Washington clash with the British army under the command of Lord Cornwallis at the Second Battle of Trenton
Isaac Collins relocates his printing press and newspaper, the New Jersey Gazette, from Burlington to Trenton, becoming the towns first publisher
The Continental Congress meets at the French Arms Tavern in Trenton to discuss the future location of the United States government
John Fitch builds and operates the first steamboat on the Delaware River between Philadelphia and Trenton
The Ladies of Trenton give George Washington a grand reception while he is en route from Philadelphia to New York to take office as the first President of the United States of America
The State Legislature selects Trenton as the seat of the capital of the State of New Jersey
Jonathan Doan and the State House Commission draw up plans for the construction of the New Jersey State House
Trenton incorporates as a city
The Ancient Free and Accepted Masons erect the Masonic Lodge, one of Trentons most prominent 18th century institutional buildings
The public offices of the United States government transfer from Philadelphia to Trenton due to a yellow fever epidemic.
The Trenton Delaware Bridge Company completes the first span connecting New Jersey and Pennsylvania across the Delaware River on the site of todays Trenton Makes bridge
Joseph Bonaparte, brother of Napoleon, flees Europe and settles in Bordentown, later occupying houses in todays South Trenton and Hamilton Township
Trenton establishes its public school system
The Trenton Delaware Falls Company incorporates with the purpose of supplying water power for industrial development in the city
The Delaware and Raritan Canal opens, permitting boats to travel between Trenton and New Brunswick
The City of Trenton becomes the seat of the newly established Mercer County
The Trenton to New Brunswick branch line of the Camden and Amboy Railroad begins operation with a station on East State Street
Dorothea Dix, social reformer and advocate for the mentally ill, successfully lobbies for the construction of the Trenton Psychiatric Hospital
John A. Roebling moves his wire rope factory from western Pennsylvania to Trenton
John Taylor and Henry Speeler establish Trentons first industrial pottery
The Trenton Waterworks Company erects the first reservoir in the city
Trenton industries begin supplying materials such as ordnance, shoes and blankets to the Union Army fighting in the Civil War
Camps Olden, Perrine, Halsted and Bayard operate in the Trenton area to recruit and house Civil War soldiers
Frank A. Magowan founds the Trenton Rubber Company, the beginning of a new industrial specialization in the city
Emily Roebling, following the serious injury of her husband, Washington A. Roebling, oversees the completion of the Brooklyn Bridge
The Cuban Giants, a Negro League Baseball team, move to Trenton with the financial backing of local entrepreneur, Walter Cook
Calvert Vaux, the English-American landscape architect, prepares designs for an expanded Riverview Cemetery
Fifty thousand people attend the opening in Hamilton of the first Inter-State Fair, the forerunner of the New Jersey State Fair
Frederick Law Olmsted, renowned landscape architect, begins work on the design of Cadwalader Park, Trentons first public park
The city celebrates the dedication of the Trenton Battle Monument, erected to commemorate the First Battle of Trenton
A group of Trenton ladies forms The Contemporary Club to stimulate an interest in science, literature, art, philanthropy and social culture
The Trenton Free Public Library opens on Academy Street
Members of the Roebling and Kuser families organize the Mercer Automobile Company to manufacture the Mercer line of automobiles
City government moves to the newly completed Trenton City Hall
The R.C. Maxwell Company installs the sign The World Takes, Trenton Makes later changed to Trenton Makes, the World Takes  on the Trenton-Morrisville Bridge
Prominent Trentonians Washington Roebling II and Stephen Blackwell die aboard the Titanic
The Trenton Marine Terminal opens, providing direct access to Trenton for deep-water vessels by means of the newly dredged Delaware River shipping channel
Mahlon Stacy Park opens, providing increased access to a beautified riverfront
The United States Army constructs Camp Dix in Burlington County to house and train soldiers enlisted to fight in World War I, many of whom hail from the Trenton area
Lenox China manufactures the first American-made set of White House china for President Woodrow Wilson
Trentons largest hotel, the Stacy-Trent, named after city founders Mahlon Stacy and William Trent, opens for business
Babe Ruth and Lou Gehrig lead a local team to victory over the Brooklyn Royal Giants in an exhibition baseball game at High School Field in Trenton
Trenton and Mercer County honor local veterans of World War I with the completion of the Soldiers and Sailors War Memorial
Mary G. Roebling becomes the President of the Trenton Trust Company and a prominent business leader in the city
The Switlik Parachute and Equipment Company becomes the major supplier of parachutes to the U.S. armed forces
Work begins on the original section of the N.J. Route 29 Freeway
Hurricane Diane causes massive flooding in the Delaware Valley, raising the river level by 20 feet in Trenton
Trenton Mayor Arthur Holland and his family take up residence in Mill Hill, sparking a restoration of this inner city neighborhood
The New Jersey State Capitol Complex, expands with the completion of new facilities for the State Library, museum and planetarium
The Roebling factories in Trenton close their doors
The people of Trenton elect Douglas H. Palmer as their first African-American Mayor
The opening of Mercer County Waterfront Park marks a significant step in the renewal of Trenton
Helis, the wayward 10-12 ft. beluga whale, becomes national news story during surprise visit to Delaware River in April
